definition: Renting computing resources - servers, storage, networking, databases and whole services - from a provider over the internet, on demand, and paying only for what is used. The provider owns and runs the hardware.
example: Creating an Azure SQL database from the portal in five minutes, and paying by the hour it exists.

definition: Infrastructure that an organisation owns and runs in its own buildings or a rack it rents. Contrast with cloud, where the provider owns the hardware. Most real estates are hybrid: some on-premises, some cloud.
Running some workloads on-premises and some in a public cloud, managed as one estate. Azure treats this as normal and provides networking, identity and management tools that span both.
Spending money up front on assets such as servers, which are then depreciated over years. On-premises infrastructure is CapEx: you size and pay for capacity before anyone uses it.

Ongoing spending on services as they are used - a monthly bill rather than an asset purchase. Cloud is OpEx, which makes cost visible and continuous, and turns cost control into a habit rather than a purchase decision.

The default cloud pricing model: resources are metered (per second, per gigabyte, per request) and billed for actual use with no up-front commitment. Reservations and savings plans trade commitment for a discount.
Capacity that grows and shrinks automatically with demand, in both directions. It is the property that lets a web shop handle a twelve-times traffic spike and then stop paying for it an hour later.
The ability of a system to handle more load by adding resources. Scaling up means a bigger machine; scaling out means more machines. Elasticity is scalability done automatically.

The lower cost per unit that comes from operating at enormous size. Hyperscalers buy hardware, energy and automation at a scale no single company can match, and competition passes part of the saving to customers.
A cloud provider operating data centres at global scale - Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud. Their size is what makes on-demand, metered computing affordable.

Moving servers to the cloud as they are, typically one on-premises machine to one virtual machine. A common first step that keeps all the patching and most of the cost, and none of the platform benefits. Treat it as a stage, not a destination.

A licensing benefit that lets existing Windows Server and SQL Server licences with Software Assurance reduce the price of the equivalent Azure services. Often the single biggest saving for a Microsoft-shaped organisation.
